summary: This program builds a list of Book objects and then loads a HashMap that pairs each book's title with its author, so any author can be found instantly from a title. It looks up "The Hobbit" and prints the matching author.

lines.text: Map is the interface for collections that store key-value pairs; you declare variables with it so the code is not tied to one particular implementation.
HashMap is the workhorse implementation of Map, and it finds a value by key very quickly no matter how many entries it holds.
The list holds Book objects rather than plain strings, so each entry keeps its title, author, and genre together.

lines.code: Book sherlock = new Book("The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes", "Arthur Conan Doyle", "Mystery");
lines.text: Each Book is created with all three pieces of information at once and stored in a named variable so it can be added to the list below.
Adding the book to the list puts it in order at the end, which is what makes the loop later able to visit every book.
The two type arguments say the keys are titles and the values are author names; a map is the right tool whenever you want to look something up by a unique label.
The enhanced for loop walks through the list one book at a time without you managing an index.
put stores the pair, using the title as the key. If two books shared a title, the second put would overwrite the first, because map keys are unique.
Holding the search term in a variable means it can be reused in both the lookup and the printed message.
get returns the value stored under that key, or null if the title was never added to the map.
Echoing the title alongside the result makes the output self-explanatory instead of a bare name.
